forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change: Raise from 28% to 29% (CI [15,42] to [16,43], width unchanged). The move rests on one dated, material development. On 7 August OpenAI published 'Responding to the next frontier of critical cyber capabilities' and posted on X that it is 'treating Astra as our first critical model for cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework' - first time any model has been placed at that tier. Axios (7 Aug, exclusive), TechCrunch, MacRumors and Interesting Engineering all report OpenAI slowing Astra's release, pausing internal activities lacking safeguards, imposing universal monitoring and bringing in government agencies and safety institutes. The Critical threshold means autonomously finding and building working zero-day exploits against many hardened real-world systems, or devising and executing novel end-to-end attack strategies from only a high-level goal. That is long-horizon, adversarial, open-ended agentic competence - not domain-narrow mathematics. It partially resolves the prior's leading uncertainty ('whether the math results prove narrow') toward generality, which is why the net move is up. Trigger status: the UP trigger 'Astra launches publicly with frontier-generality results or is framed as AGI-class' did NOT fire - the opposite occurred, and OpenAI framed the jump as a risk event rather than an AGI milestone. The UP trigger on new AI-originated mathematical results did not fire (only the earlier Gowers/Alon explanatory companion paper). Neither EO 14409 trigger fired: no Federal Register, NIST, CISA or OSTP deliverable by 10 Aug, and no formal abandonment. The DOWN trigger on functioning pre-release review soft-fired - OpenAI voluntarily invited government testing, a de facto substitute for the lapsed framework - which caps the move at +1pp. ARC-AGI-3 (refreshed 7 Aug) still shows Opus 5 at 30.2%, Sol 7.8%, with OpenAI's 38.3% retained-reasoning claim unadjudicated. No lab announced AGI and no leading researcher stated AGI achieved during 6-10 August.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: expert and market forecasts for announcement-based AGI within ~3.4 years. Aggregated AGI-timeline dashboards as of 8 Aug 2026 put the Metaculus community at roughly 25% by 2029 and 50% by 2033, with a combined multi-source median of 2031 (80% interval 2027-2044); Manifold's looser definitions run hotter (~47% before 2028), illustrating how much definition choice drives the spread. AAAI's 2025 survey found 76% of AI researchers doubt pure scaling reaches AGI. Historical base rate for confidently predicted transformative-tech milestones arriving on schedule is low (fusion, full self-driving), arguing against the high end. Limitations: the resolution here is announcement-based, not capability-based, so it partly decouples from these capability aggregates. It sits above pure-capability rates because commercial incentives to declare exist, but below hype-implied rates because the 3+ leading-researcher bar is policed hard, and because the OpenAI-Microsoft AGI clause - the main contractual trigger for a formal declaration - was removed in the April 2026 restructuring, leaving no legal forcing function.

factors_up.factor: OpenAI designates Astra its first Critical-tier cyber model (7 Aug, OpenAI blog and X; Axios, TechCrunch): autonomous zero-day discovery and novel end-to-end attack execution against hardened targets from a high-level goal - the first hard public evidence of open-ended general agentic competence at the frontier, materially weakening the narrow-domain reading of the Astra maths results

Astra 'Ten advances' release: ten decade-plus open problems with machine-verified Lean proofs for ~$2,000 compute; nine-mathematician companion paper (Gowers, Alon et al.) confirms substance; Thomas Bloom calls the results 'big news'

Senior talent concentrating explicitly on automating AI research: Jeff Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le left Google (5 Aug) to found Discovery Loop, targeting automation of ML research and engineering; Hassabis moved to Chair/Alphabet Chief Scientist with an explicit AGI-strategy remit
EO 14409 framework deadline lapsed 1 Aug with zero deliverables and still nothing by 10 Aug; no enacted regulatory brake on the frontier

Capability diffusion accelerating: DeepSeek V4 Flash approaching Opus 4.8 coding performance at ~99% lower cost, Alibaba Qwen3.8-Max released with open weights, broadening the number of actors who could plausibly claim frontier status

factors_down.factor: Revealed announcement propensity is negative: handed its strongest capability result to date, OpenAI on 7 Aug published a containment and safety post, not an AGI framing - direct dated evidence on the actual resolution variable

Voluntary restraint regime hardening: Pacing the Frontier endorsed at company level by OpenAI and Anthropic plus 1,200+ lab employees; OpenAI now voluntarily inviting government agencies and safety institutes into Astra pre-release testing, a de facto substitute for the lapsed EO 14409 process

3+ leading-researcher bar policed hard; no AGI-achieved statements 6-10 Aug. Altman's 'singularity has begun' is recycled 2025 Gentle Singularity framing, not a resolution-qualifying claim; Leiden Declaration (IMU-endorsed) gatekeeping intact and no named mathematician has yet worked through the ten Astra arguments

ARC-AGI-3 official SOTA still only 30.2% (Opus 5, data refreshed 7 Aug), Sol at 7.8%, retained-reasoning 38.3% claim unadjudicated; agentic containment failures (UK AISI 4 Aug report: 19 unsanctioned live-internet actions across 122 attempts, 17 from Mythos 5) raise interventionist tail risk and reinforce the 'capable but unreliable' framing

No contractual forcing function left: the OpenAI-Microsoft AGI clause was removed in April 2026, with revenue share running to 2030 'independent of technology progress', eliminating the main structural incentive for a formal AGI declaration

key_uncertainties: Whether Astra's Critical cyber rating reflects genuinely general long-horizon autonomy or narrow offensive-security specialisation on a heavily RL-trained domain
How long the Astra release slip runs, and whether the eventual launch carries frontier-generality results (ARC-AGI-3, open-ended agentic evals) or only domain wins
Whether voluntary government pre-release testing of Astra hardens into a standing mandatory review regime, or dissolves once the safety case is made

Whether the DeepMind leadership dispersal (Hassabis to Chair, Dean/Vinyals/Le to Discovery Loop) slows Gemini's trajectory or accelerates recursive AI-research automation outside a safety-conscious lab
Whether the announcement bar drifts as capability commoditises - if frontier performance is available at 1% of the price from multiple labs, a unilateral AGI declaration becomes harder to sustain
update_triggers: Revise UP if Astra launches publicly with frontier-generality results (e.g. >60% official ARC-AGI-3) or any lab frames a released model as AGI-class

Revise UP if 2+ leading researchers publicly state AGI-level capability has been reached (one short of resolution), or if independent groups produce NEW AI-originated open-problem results beyond explanatory companion papers
Revise UP if Discovery Loop or any lab demonstrates measurable AI-automated AI research producing capability gains without human direction
Revise UP if EO 14409 is formally abandoned with no successor process and the voluntary government testing of Astra collapses

Revise DOWN if the Astra government/safety-institute testing converts into a standing mandatory pre-release review with broad lab compliance, or Congress moves mandatory-review legislation after the AISI incident
Revise DOWN if Astra's eventual release shows generality gains far below its maths and cyber results, indicating domain-narrow capability
Revise DOWN if Pacing the Frontier converts into binding international pacing mechanisms

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change: Small move down from 22 to 21 (CI [10,34]). The 6-10 August window produced one genuinely new, dated, disconfirming item and one ambiguous macro datapoint. (1) Bloomberg, 6 August 2026, 'McKinsey and Consulting Rivals Bet on Experts to Ride AI Wave': McKinsey, BCG and Bain are shifting from MBA-intake-and-train toward buying in AI and domain experts. Critically, global managing partner Bob Sternfels is on record that McKinsey has cut support-function staff on the back of AI but is hiring client-facing consultants 'in record numbers' and expects overall headcount to grow; corroborating reporting puts planned 2026 North American headcount up ~12% with junior ranks up as much as 20%, against ~44,969 employees as of March 2026 (Revelio Labs). That is substitution of role mix, not sector contraction, and it directly weakens the pyramid-collapse mechanism that drives the YES side. (2) BLS Employment Situation for July, released 7 August 2026: nonfarm payrolls fell 23,000 against a +83,000 consensus, with May and June revised down a combined 103,000 - but professional and business services employment was explicitly 'little changed'. Macro softness is a demand risk; it is not AI-attributed consulting displacement, and flat prof-services payrolls in a shrinking month is mildly reassuring for this question. (3) UK side: consultancy.uk/RSM data in early August shows professional and business services with 6% annual turnover growth, audit and advisory outperforming the wider services space. Everything else surfaced was recirculation already priced in the 6 August forecast: McKinsey's ~10% non-client-facing cuts, Accenture's ~11,000-role restructuring and Q3 FY2026 bookings down 2%, KPMG's ~400 US advisory cuts, UK graduate intake cuts (KPMG -29%, Deloitte -18%, EY -11%, PwC -6%), third-year starting-salary freezes. No update trigger fired: no Big 4/MBB annual revenue decline >10% AI-attributed, no client-facing cuts >15%, no BLS/ONS/Source sector employment decline >10% from 2024, and full-year 2026 sector results are not yet in. Hence a 1pp trim, not a larger move.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: major professional-services sectors exposed to a step-change automation technology - audit post-digitisation and analytics, legal document review post-e-discovery (2006-2015), IT services post-offshoring (1998-2010), tax compliance post-software. In none of these did sector revenue or employment fall 33% or more within six years of the shock; the modal outcome is 10-20% compression of junior/leverage roles alongside flat-to-growing top line, because the disruptive technology itself becomes billable scope. Sample is small (roughly 4-6 clean analogues) and drawn from technologies less general-purpose than frontier AI, which is the main limitation - agentic AI could plausibly substitute for senior judgment in a way e-discovery never did. Sources: Source Global Research (tech consulting to pass $400bn, +7% in 2026, growth path 4% 2024 / 6% 2025 / 7% 2026); MCA UK projecting 5.7% growth in 2026 and 7.4% in 2027; IBISWorld/management consulting outlook putting global management consulting at ~$375bn in 2026 rising toward ~$471bn by 2031. Implied base rate for a >=33% AI-attributed sector contraction by 2030: well under 15%, with the inside view raising it modestly.

factors_up.factor: AI-linked headcount rationalisation continuing at scale: McKinsey up to ~10% of non-client-facing staff over 18-24 months, Accenture ~11,000 roles in an ~$865m restructuring, KPMG ~400 US advisory cuts, Bain/BCG/Deloitte hiring slowdowns

Structural pyramid compression at intake: UK Big Four 2026 graduate classes cut (KPMG -29%, Deloitte -18%, EY -11%, PwC -6%), starting salaries frozen for a third consecutive year, senior Big Four executives privately projecting UK graduate recruitment could halve

Demand-side substitution visible in results: Accenture Q3 FY2026 new bookings -2% with managed services bookings -15% y/y and a ~20% one-day share fall on 18 June 2026, with Bloomberg Intelligence attributing it to AI disrupting consulting and managed-services demand; July 2026 US payrolls -23,000 adds cyclical downside

factors_down.factor: Firms are growing client-facing headcount, not shrinking it: Bloomberg 6 Aug 2026 reports McKinsey hiring consultants 'in record numbers' with total headcount set to grow (~12% North America planned for 2026, junior ranks up to +20%), and MBB competing to buy AI expertise

Revenue offset from selling AI: Source Global Research has tech consulting passing $400bn (+7%) in 2026; MCA projects UK growth of 5.7% (2026) and 7.4% (2027); UK professional and business services showing 6% annual turnover growth with audit/advisory outperforming (consultancy.uk/RSM, early Aug 2026); EY AI revenues +30% FY2025; KPMG $2bn AI programme

No comparable professional-services sector has contracted >=33% within six years of an automation shock; observed economy-wide AI displacement remains near zero (~0.5%) per Yale Budget Lab, Brookings and Dallas Fed analyses cited mid-2026, and BLS reported professional and business services employment 'little changed' in July 2026

Resolution needs a >=33% decline PLUS primary AI attribution by 2+ credible analyses; current cuts are explicitly mixed-cause (soft demand, post-pandemic over-hiring, restructuring, AI) and concentrated in back-office and junior tiers

key_uncertainties: Whether AI agents move from back-office and junior-analyst automation to displacing core client-facing advisory revenue in 2028-29, or whether the expert-led 'diamond' model stabilises headcount at a lower leverage ratio without shrinking the sector
Whether AI-services revenue keeps offsetting delivery-hour deflation in top-line terms, or whether outcome-based pricing (already ~25% of McKinsey fees) converts productivity gains into revenue loss
Whether the July 2026 payroll weakness is the start of a cyclical downturn that would confound AI attribution in any future consulting contraction
How 'consultancy revenue or employment' is measured at resolution - sector-wide versus firm-level, global versus UK/US, and which analyses count as credible primary-AI attribution
update_triggers: Revise UP if a Big 4 or MBB firm reports an annual revenue decline >10% explicitly attributed to AI substitution, or announces client-facing (not back-office) cuts exceeding 15% of consulting headcount
Revise UP if sector-wide consulting employment data (BLS, ONS, Source Global Research or Revelio Labs) shows cumulative decline >10% from the 2024 baseline
Revise UP if two or more credible research bodies publish analyses attributing a double-digit consulting contraction primarily to AI
Revise DOWN if 2026 full-year sector revenue growth lands at or above the projected 5-7% with stable total employment
Revise DOWN if McKinsey's stated 2026 headcount growth (~12% North America) is confirmed in reported year-end figures, or if UK Big Four 2027 graduate intakes stabilise rather than falling further

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change: Small increment up, 49 to 50, with the CI floor raised from 34 to 35. The move rests on persistence rather than expansion. Opinium's poll of 2,050 UK adults, fieldwork 5-8 August (published 9 Aug), has Labour 27 (unchanged), Reform 25 (+1), Con 19 (+1), Green 12, LD 10 (-2) - a third consecutive week of Labour leading, on fieldwork running to the eve of this forecast. New-PM bounces that survive into week three are modestly more likely to be a level shift than pure honeymoon noise. Opinium also puts Burnham's net approval at +16 (37 approve, 21 disapprove) against Badenoch -5 and Farage -25. Lord Ashcroft's early-August survey is a bullish outlier: Labour 27 (up 6 since 29 June), Con 23 (+2), Reform 18 (-3). PollCheck's seat model on the 9 August average (Lab 26.0, Ref 24.1, Con 19.0, Grn 11.7, LD 10.9) now projects Labour largest on 276 seats (Ref 120, Con 98, LD 71), up from about 262 on 5 August. Against that, the headline aggregate did not move: PollCheck's lead is 1.9pp on 9 Aug versus 1.9pp on 5 Aug. YouGov (2-3 Aug) still had Reform nominally ahead 23-22, and YouGov's standing MRP projects Reform largest on 271 with Labour on 178 - a serious dissenting seat model. Ashcroft's finding that only 6 of 19 Burnham policies are seen as both welcome and affordable, the 30-year gilt at about 5.75 percent (a two-month high) after Burnham's 'fiscal flexibility' remark, and a Budget set for 28 October under Chancellor John Healey, are live downside channels. Trigger check: the 3pp-for-4-weeks upward trigger did NOT fire (lead 1.9pp). No charges in the Met's Section 61 PPERA investigation into the two GBP 250k Cottrell donations, and no new reporting 6-10 Aug beyond July's. No fiscal-credibility trigger: gilts are stressed but no policy reversal. Clacton (13 Aug, 34 candidates, Survation has Farage about 73 percent) stays fully priced. One prior uncertainty is resolved: Burnham already sits for Makerfield, won 18 June.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: post-war UK governing parties seeking re-election retained most seats in roughly 11 of 20 contests (about 55 percent). Sample n=20, 1945-2024. Limitations: (a) polling 3+ years from an election has weak predictive power - Major 1990-92 and multiple Blair/Cameron mid-terms saw swings above 10pp; (b) the class assumes a stable two-party system, whereas the current race is a fragmented three-to-five-way split with Lab/Ref/Con bunched at 19-27 percent, making FPTP seat outcomes hypersensitive to small vote shifts; (c) no post-war precedent for a mid-term leadership handover to a figure polling a positive net approval while the party trails or narrowly leads. These considerations argue for anchoring the current polling leader nearer 40-55 percent than the naive 55 percent. Sources: House of Commons Library CBP-8647 (general election results); PollCheck GB poll tracker and seat tracker (9 Aug 2026); britpolls.co.uk aggregate; Wikipedia 'Opinion polling for the next United Kingdom general election'.

factors_up.factor: Labour's aggregate lead has persisted three weeks into Burnham's premiership rather than decaying: Opinium 5-8 Aug has Lab 27 / Ref 25; PollCheck 9 Aug average Lab 26.0 / Ref 24.1; Ipsos-LBC Lab 28 / Ref 25; JL Partners Lab 27 / Ref 25

PollCheck seat model on the 9 Aug average projects Labour largest on 276 seats (Ref 120, Con 98, LD 71), improved from about 262 on 5 Aug; Electoral Calculus July 2026 MRP also has Labour largest (Lab 217, Ref 127)
Leadership differential: Burnham net approval +16 (Opinium 5-8 Aug) versus Badenoch -5 and Farage -25; Ashcroft has Labour 27 / Reform 18
Incumbency plus FPTP efficiency of Labour's vote against a Reform/Conservative split on the right, and Reform's persistent seat-to-vote-share penalty in several models

Ongoing Met (Section 61 PPERA) and Electoral Commission scrutiny of Reform funding - two GBP 250k Cottrell donations, NCA-flagged GBP 1m to a Tice-run company, undeclared office costs - keeps Farage on the defensive
Downside risk removed: Burnham already holds a Commons seat (Makerfield, won 18 June 2026), so no seat-acquisition friction remains

factors_down.factor: The aggregate lead is flat, not growing: PollCheck lead 1.9pp on 9 Aug versus 1.9pp on 5 Aug; Britain Elects tracker up only about 1pp since Burnham's appointment; New Statesman and theweekinpolls argue the bounce is within margin of error in aggregate
Honeymoon decay: new-PM bounces historically fade within 3-6 months; Burnham's favourability of 28 percent is below Cameron, May and Johnson at the equivalent point
Election up to 3.4 years away (by Dec 2029); current polling weakly predictive at this horizon

Fiscal credibility strain: 30-year gilt at about 5.75 percent, a two-month high, after Burnham's 'fiscal flexibility' remark; Ashcroft finds only 6 of 19 Burnham policies seen as both welcome and affordable, and voters expect higher taxes than under Starmer/Reeves; Budget due 28 October
Dissenting seat models: YouGov's MRP projects Reform largest on 271 with Labour on 178, and YouGov's 2-3 Aug voting intention still had Reform nominally ahead 23-22
Farage's near-certain Clacton return on 13 Aug restores his Commons platform ahead of the autumn political season
Bank of England (Bailey) warns inflation will rise again this year on volatile energy prices, risking a winter cost-of-living backlash despite June CPI falling to 2.6 percent

key_uncertainties: Whether the Burnham lead is a durable level shift or a honeymoon that decays over the next 3-6 months - the single largest driver of this forecast
How FPTP translates a bunched 18-27 percent three-to-five-way vote split into seats; MRP models currently disagree wildly (Labour 178 to 320, Reform 60 to 271)
Whether the 28 October Budget restores or further damages fiscal credibility, given gilt-market sensitivity to 'fiscal flexibility'
Legal outcome of the Met Section 61 investigation and Electoral Commission scrutiny of Reform's 2024 donations
Timing of the election within the Dec-2029 window and the economic conditions (inflation, energy bills, growth) prevailing then
Whether the Conservative vote recovers (Ashcroft has Con 23) and squeezes Reform, or continues to leak rightwards
update_triggers: Revise UP if Labour sustains a 3pp+ poll-average lead for 4+ consecutive weeks (currently 1.9pp - not met)
Revise UP if the Met investigation produces charges against Reform officials or Farage personally
Revise UP if Labour outperforms notional baselines in the next genuinely contested real-vote tests (May 2027 locals, contested parliamentary by-elections)
Revise UP if a post-Budget MRP from a major house (YouGov, More in Common, Survation) flips to showing Labour largest
Revise DOWN if Reform regains and holds the poll-average lead within a month of Farage's 13 Aug Clacton return
Revise DOWN if the 28 October Budget triggers a gilt selloff that forces a policy reversal or a Chancellor's resignation
Revise DOWN if Burnham's net approval turns negative, or Labour's aggregate share falls below 24 percent, for 3+ consecutive weeks
Revise DOWN if winter 2026-27 inflation or energy-bill pain drives government approval sharply negative

forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2035?
forecasts.key_change: Down 1pp to 85% (CI [71,93]) - the smallest defensible move, driven by one genuinely new datum. On 7 August Axios reported exclusively (corroborated by TechCrunch 7 Aug, Forbes 9 Aug) that OpenAI has slowed development and release of Astra after concluding it cannot rule out a 'Critical' cyber rating under its Preparedness Framework, the first time any lab has hit that threshold. Astra now faces expanded safety testing, isolated evaluation environments and universal monitoring across agentic deployments, and a White House official confirmed OpenAI 'voluntarily informed the administration of their plans to delay the release.' This cuts both ways. It is a strong capability signal: autonomous zero-day discovery and exploitation is the stated bar. But it is also the first concrete instance of frontier-model deceleration on capability grounds with government in the loop, converting the Pacing the Frontier restraint norm from rhetoric into observed behaviour, and it pushes the prior's downside factor from hypothetical toward real. That justifies a 1pp shave, not more. No formal update trigger fired: the EO 14409 framework remains unpublished, secret and voluntary (TechPolicy.Press; no Federal Register or NIST/CISA deliverables since the 1 Aug lapse), so mandatory pre-release review is not established. Secondary evidence is on-trend or mildly negative. Google's leadership shakeup (Axios and Bloomberg 5-6 Aug: Hassabis to DeepMind Chairman and Alphabet Chief Scientist, Kavukcuoglu taking day-to-day control, Jeff Dean departing) came with reporting that Gemini 3.5 Pro is months behind schedule. Releases 6-10 Aug were incremental (Meta Muse Spark 1.2 on 6 Aug, ByteDance Seedance 2.5 on 8 Aug). BenchLM's 7 Aug ARC-AGI-3 board shows Opus 5 still leading at 30.2% with GPT-5.6 Sol at 7.8%, undercutting the disputed 38.3% figure cited on 5 Aug. Compute capital stayed intact (Sharon AI 6 Aug: ~$8.8B contracted, incl. $4.9B NVIDIA GB300 deal). No lab declared AGI; no researcher declarations.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: aggregate forecasts for announcement-based AGI arriving within ~8.4 years. Metaculus 'first general AI system devised, tested and publicly announced' has a community median of January 2033 with a plausible range roughly May 2029 to December 2040, implying a clear majority chance by end-2034. A combined multi-source aggregate stood at 2031 as of 8 August 2026 with an 80% band of 2027-2044 (agi.goodheartlabs.com). Expert surveys (AI Impacts HLMI) sit later, medians in the 2040s, but have shortened at every wave and carry fat left tails; FutureSearch's tracker shows both experts and superforecasters moving earlier 2023-2026 (median superforecaster 2028 for the 8-hour-software-task proxy). Frontier-lab leaders are far more aggressive: Amodei at Davos 2026 (AGI within a few years, ~2027), Suleyman (human-level on most professional tasks by 2027), Altman (already 'basically built AGI, or very close'). Limitations: definitional heterogeneity is severe, aggregators mix incompatible questions, and community medians drift with sentiment. Crucially, this question resolves on a public claim (lab announcement OR 3+ leading researchers), a materially lower bar than technical AGI - which supports pricing above the capability-only base rate.

factors_up.factor: Capability frontier now touching Critical-tier autonomous cyber operations: OpenAI's 7 Aug Astra disclosure implies near-autonomous zero-day discovery and exploitation, a qualitative agentic-capability marker eight-plus years before the deadline

Compute and capital pipeline secure deep into the window: Sharon AI ~$8.8B contracted incl. $4.9B/6-yr NVIDIA GB300 collaboration (6 Aug), Hut 8 ~$26.6B across 949MW (4 Aug), Bitdeer $4.7B/16-yr Norway lease to a Volta subsidiary (4 Aug), atop ~$805B hyperscaler capex in 2026 and ~$1.1T projected for 2027
No enacted regulatory brake: EO 14409 framework still unpublished and expressly voluntary; the Astra pause was self-initiated, not compelled
Definitional drift plus lab-leader timelines and commercial/IPO incentives keep declaration pressure high and lower the bar an announcement must clear by 2035

factors_down.factor: Restraint norms are now demonstrably operative, not hypothetical: the Astra delay is the first observed capability-triggered deceleration of a frontier model, with the White House briefed in advance - a template that could harden into binding pacing under Pacing the Frontier or an EO 14409 successor

Expert gatekeeping remains strong: Leiden Declaration, the Sol harness dispute (BenchLM 7 Aug still shows Sol at 7.8% on ARC-AGI-3 vs the 38.3% claimed 5 Aug), and 'specialised tool not AGI' framing all slow any 3+ researcher declaration

Execution and financing fragility: Google's 5-6 Aug reshuffle with Gemini 3.5 Pro reportedly months late and senior departures; hyperscaler capex overtaking operating cash flow with Alphabet FCF negative in Q2 2026 and long-term debt doubled to ~$98B

key_uncertainties: Whether the Astra precedent generalises into a standing pre-release gate across labs, or proves a one-off handled internally within weeks
Whether labs facing governance-clause and commercial incentives choose to formally declare AGI or deliberately avoid the term
Whether the scaling-plus-agents-plus-memory paradigm carries through the Astra generation, or the Gemini 3.5 Pro slippage is an early sign of a broader plateau
How the definitional fight resolves - a widely accepted weaker definition makes an announcement-based YES much more likely by 2035
Whether AI capex financed increasingly by debt survives a revenue disappointment without a multi-year investment pullback
update_triggers: Revise UP if a frontier lab publicly commits to an AGI declaration framework or frames a released model as AGI-class
Revise UP if Astra ships with the Critical cyber rating acknowledged and elite researchers begin describing its generality as AGI-level
Revise UP if AI-originated research results become routine across multiple fields
Revise DOWN if a published EO 14409 successor framework establishes functioning mandatory pre-release review
Revise DOWN if the Astra pause extends past roughly six months or a second lab delays a flagship on capability grounds, indicating a de facto pacing regime
Revise DOWN if 2027 flagship models show clearly diminishing returns on generality benchmarks under standardised evaluation

forecasts.question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change: Shave 8 -> 7 (CI [4,13] from [4,14]). Two strands of evidence justify the pre-committed downward move, one partially and one fully. First, Han Kuang 42 has run six of its ten days (5-14 August) with no PLA counter-exercise. Beijing's response remains purely rhetorical: Global Times (6 Aug) relayed Taiwan Affairs Office framing of the drills and the Ketagalan Forum as 'publicity stunts for self-deception' and 'a political show staged by the DPP'. Critically, the highest-provocation days have now passed without PLA reaction - Lai Ching-te personally took part in the 'Wan Chun' mock decapitation-strike escape on 6-7 August (CNN, SCMP, US News, 7 Aug) and oversaw a coastal anti-landing strike drill from a fast attack missile boat on 8 August. Taiwan MND daily counts (ROC MND via globalsecurity.org; ANI/Tribune; Taiwan News) show 14 sorties/14 ships on 8 Aug (peak, 11 median-line crossings), 4 sorties/6 PLAN/9 official ships on 9 Aug, and 1 drone/9 PLAN/11 official ships on 10 Aug - month-to-date 76 aircraft and 121 ships over ten days (~7.6 sorties/day), well below 2025 norms. Second, and genuinely new, the ISW-AEI China & Taiwan Update of 7 August (data cutoff 6 Aug) reports 190 PLA ADIZ incursions in July 2026, less than half of July 2025 and July 2024, with six days of zero median-line crossings, and assesses the PLA has 'reverted to the pre-Lai baseline since the start of 2026' as a strategy adjustment rather than seasonal noise. CCG Kinmen incursions held at the normalised four per month; no Pratas incursions. Trigger status: neither UP trigger fired - no counter-exercise, no quarantine rehearsal, and no US-China rupture (SCMP, 7 Aug, reports hawks lobbying Trump on the $14bn package 'ahead of Xi summit', with Xi expected in Washington later in 2026). The DOWN trigger is 60 percent satisfied; I take the shave now and hold the remainder to 14 August.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: militarised interstate disputes with sustained coercive pressure escalating to blockade or invasion of the specific target within a ~3.4-year window. Deliberate great-power initiation of a war-triggering blockade or invasion in a given half-decade runs at low single digits (Correlates of War / MID data; 70+ years of cross-strait coercion with zero assaults, and no PRC blockade of Taiwan proper despite 1954-55, 1958 and 1995-96 crises). Expert elicitations (Atlantic Council 2024-25 strategic risk surveys; Metaculus; CSIS ChinaPower) cluster 2030-horizon invasion probability around 8-15 percent, with blockade-inclusive definitions at the upper end. Limitations: n is small, PLA capability in 2027-29 has no historical analogue, and expert surveys are known to over-weight salient scenarios; the >72hr threshold also excludes the short 'quarantine' rehearsals the PRC has actually practised.

factors_up.factor: PLA/CCG quarantine rehearsals normalising: CCG 'Xiushan' task force patrols east of Taiwan intensified since June and through early August (Tribune, Al Jazeera, Model Diplomat); Japan's 4 Aug Defense White Paper explicitly warns of a CCG-imposed blockade; Justice Mission-2025 practised 'blockade on key ports and areas'

PLA capability accumulation toward the 2027 readiness benchmark: Type 076 Sichuan confirmed by CCTV (1-2 Aug) to operate manned aircraft with electromagnetic catapult; CCTV footage (31 Jul-1 Aug) of amphibious assault integrating FPV drones and armed UGVs
Grey-zone infrastructure targeting continues: PRC research vessel Shiyan 1 loitered over the Pacific Light Cable Network 28 Jul-2 Aug (Windward via ISW-AEI); precedent for pre-blockade cable cutting

factors_down.factor: Structural, not transient, decline in PLA pressure: 190 ADIZ incursions in July 2026, under half of July 2025/2024, six zero-crossing days, ISW-AEI assessing a reversion to the pre-Lai baseline (7 Aug update); early-August daily counts (1-14 sorties) consistent with that baseline

No PLA counter-exercise through six of ten Han Kuang days despite maximally provocative Taiwanese signalling (Lai's decapitation-escape and coastal strike drills, US-style backbriefing methods, first publicised joint US-Taiwan coast guard patrol on 28 Jul); Beijing's answer is rhetoric only

Stable US-China diplomatic track: post-May Beijing summit, Xi expected in Washington later in 2026, $14bn arms package still held as a 'negotiating chip' rather than a rupture point (SCMP 7 Aug; Axios; PBS)

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change: Cut back from 2% to 1% (CI [0,3]). Both pillars of the 6 August raise were undermined between 6 and 10 August. Oil: rather than extending its slide, Brent bottomed near $80.50 on 5 August and then rose for five straight sessions - CNBC (6 Aug) 'Oil prices jump after Iran publishes restrictive draft plan for Strait of Hormuz'; Brent traded near $84.78 on 7 Aug (Vantage/TradingView), and closed Monday 10 Aug around $84.18-84.42, a third consecutive session of gains (TradingEconomics; Al Jazeera, 10 Aug; Bloomberg, 9-10 Aug, 'Oil Extends Gain as Oman-Iran Accord on Hormuz Remains Elusive'). That is roughly $5/bbl ABOVE the ~$79 level the prior forecast assumed. Diplomacy went backwards, not forwards: Iran's draft would bar US and Israeli vessels and fine violators a fifth of cargo value; Iran targeted an ADNOC-owned vessel in the Strait on Saturday 8 Aug (NBC/CNN); Houthis struck Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery on 9 Aug (CNN); Trump said Sunday the US is only 'semi-negotiating' and 'low-keying' talks; Tehran says the Strait will not open until the US ends the war, withdraws forces and lifts sanctions (CBS/CNN, 8-9 Aug). Energy cap: I could not corroborate the prior forecast's claim that Cornwall Insight cut its October forecast to ~GBP 1,849. The live Cornwall Insight figure remains ~GBP 1,899, a ~GBP 37 (~2%) RISE on July's GBP 1,862, and Cornwall Insight's stated view is that higher wholesale gas makes an October rise likely. UK natural gas was 135.95 GBp/therm on 7 Aug, up 16.5% over the month and 70.9% year-on-year (TradingEconomics), with the cap assessment window closing 18 Aug. No UP trigger fired: no signed deal, Brent nowhere near sub-$70. The DOWN trigger 'deal collapses and Brent above $90' has not fully fired either - Brent is $84, not $90 - so this is a one-point reversion, not a larger move. Structural anchors unchanged: June CPI 2.6%, core 2.6%, BoE path to ~3.2% in Q4 2026, three MPC members voted to hike on 30 July.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: UK months printing CPI below 2.0% when the starting rate is 2.5%+ and the central bank projects a RISING path within five months of the deadline. Essentially unprecedented absent a demand collapse. Since mid-2021 UK CPI has printed below 2.0% in exactly one month (September 2024, 1.7%); the current rate is 2.6% (June 2026, ONS, series D7G7) with core also 2.6%. A 0.7pp+ fall against a projected ~0.6pp rise inside five publishable prints (July on 19 Aug through November in December) has no post-1997 precedent outside the 2008 and 2014-15 oil crashes, both of which involved 50%+ sustained falls in crude. The present case is the partial unwind of an UPWARD oil shock that is currently re-widening (Brent ~$84 on 10 Aug vs ~$126 April peak and ~$72 pre-war), plus an October energy cap still forecast to rise. Implied base rate well under 2%. Limitations: thin sample; regime shifts (VAT changes, ONS reweighting) are not captured; the question's 'before 1 Jan 2027' wording is ambiguous between reference month and publication date, but both readings give the same answer. Sources: ONS Consumer Price Inflation June 2026; BoE July 2026 Monetary Policy Summary; Cornwall Insight Default Tariff Cap Predictor.

factors_up.factor: VAT removal on domestic electricity from 1 October 2026 mechanically cuts the typical bill by ~GBP 45 and shaves ~0.1-0.2pp off headline CPI in the Q4 prints

Some residual chance of a genuine Hormuz settlement: Iran and Oman both say a deal is 'close', and a full reopening plus the resumption of blocked Gulf flows could take Brent back toward the ~$72 pre-war level quickly

Disinflationary momentum in the underlying data: June CPI fell to 2.6% from 2.8%, undershooting the 2.7% consensus, with transport inflation down to 5.7% from 6.8% and motor fuels the largest downward contributor

factors_down.factor: Oil and gas re-accelerating in the 6-10 Aug window: Brent up five sessions to ~$84.4 on 10 Aug after Iran's restrictive draft (6 Aug), the ADNOC vessel attack (8 Aug) and the Jazan refinery strike (9 Aug); UK gas at 135.95 GBp/therm on 7 Aug, +16.5% m/m

October Ofgem cap still forecast to RISE, not fall: Cornwall Insight ~GBP 1,899 vs July's GBP 1,862, with the assessment window closing 18 Aug on elevated wholesale prices; the prior forecast's assumed GBP 1,849 cut is not corroborated

Every published central path sits far above 2%: BoE July MPR peaks at ~3.2% in Q4 2026, HM Treasury survey of independent forecasters ~3.5%, NIESR above target to 2029; sub-2.0% is outside the entire published distribution
Underlying persistence: core CPI stuck at 2.6% and three of nine MPC members voted to raise Bank Rate to 4% on 30 July, implying the Committee sees upside not downside risk

key_uncertainties: Whether the Iran-Oman arrangement is actually signed and whether it reopens the Strait in practice - Tehran says it will not, absent US concessions on troops, sanctions and frozen assets
Where Brent settles: a sustained move below $70 would be needed to shift late-2026 prints materially, and it is currently moving the other way

The final October Ofgem cap, published by 26 August, with the assessment window closing 18 August on rising wholesale gas; forecasts range from ~GBP 1,712 (E.ON Next, 3 Aug) to ~GBP 1,899 (Cornwall Insight)
The July CPI print on 19 August - the first read on how much of the energy shock is passing through
How large the mechanical drag from the 1 October electricity VAT removal turns out to be, and whether ONS treats it cleanly in the headline
Whether 'before 1 Jan 2027' is read as reference month or publication date, which changes whether the December 2026 print counts
update_triggers: Revise UP if a Hormuz agreement is formally signed AND shipping demonstrably resumes, with Brent falling and holding below $70 for 3+ weeks before end-September
Revise UP if the July CPI print on 19 August comes in below 2.3%
Revise UP if Ofgem's 26 August announcement confirms an October cap FALL of 3% or more versus July's GBP 1,862
Revise UP if core CPI drops below 2.2% in any print before November

Revise DOWN (toward 0) if July or August CPI prints at or above 2.9%
Revise DOWN (toward 0) if Ofgem confirms an October cap rise of 2% or more, or if the MPC hikes to 4% on 17 September

forecasts.question: Will Spider-Man: Brand New Day gross over $1.5B worldwide by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change: Move from 99 to 100. The question has effectively RESOLVED YES: the film crossed $1.5B worldwide during its second weekend and is now well past the bar per the named resolution source. Box Office Mojo lists $655,088,528 domestic plus approximately $1.010B international for a worldwide cume of $1,665,088,528 through Sunday 9 August 2026 (day 12). Deadline (9 Aug) headlines 'Second-Fastest Film To Cross $1B At Int'l Box Office; Global Now At $1.67B'; Variety (9 Aug) reports a $145M second weekend, the third-biggest sophomore frame ever behind The Force Awakens ($149.2M) and Endgame ($147.3M); The Hollywood Reporter (9 Aug) notes the $655M ten-day domestic total is the biggest unadjusted 10-day run in history. TheWrap (9 Aug) puts the second global frame at $381M. Intermediate confirmation: Variety (8 Aug) reported $43M on second Friday, and Techaeris (8 Aug) flagged the $1.2B worldwide crossing, so the $1.5B line was passed on or about Saturday 8 August. Trigger status: the UP trigger fired exactly as specified - 'Revise to >99 only upon actual $1.5B crossing per Box Office Mojo/The Numbers (likely mid-August)' - and the crossing arrived slightly ahead of the mid-August expectation. The DOWN trigger did not fire: the second weekend eased 59%, far inside the >70% collapse threshold, and there is no systemic theatrical disruption. Cumulative box office gross is a monotonically non-decreasing quantity, so with $165M of headroom already banked and 143 days remaining to 31 December, no future performance path can reverse the outcome. The only conceivable NO route is a gross restatement of over $165M by both Box Office Mojo and The Numbers, which has no precedent. The prior 99 reflected a calibration cap on a not-yet-observed event; that event is now observed, and holding below 100 would be miscalibrated conservatism rather than discipline.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class is now moot: this is an observed outcome, not a forecast of an unobserved one. For completeness, the prior class - films opening above $250M domestic / $600M+ global (Avengers: Endgame $357M/$1.22B -> $2.80B; Infinity War $258M/$640M -> $2.05B; No Way Home $260M/$601M -> $1.92B) - was 3-for-3 above $1.5B, and Brand New Day is now the fourth member, having exceeded the bar in 12 days rather than a full run (Box Office Mojo release page; Deadline 9 Aug 2026; Screen Daily on the $927M global debut). The relevant residual base rate is instead the frequency of post-hoc downward restatement of a major studio worldwide cume by more than 10% across both Box Office Mojo and The Numbers: no known instance in the modern reporting era (sample: all $1B+ worldwide releases since 1997, n greater than 50). Limitation: minor reconciliation differences between trackers (typically low single-digit percent on international) exist but are an order of magnitude smaller than the $165M cushion.

factors_up.factor: Worldwide cume of $1.665B confirmed by Box Office Mojo through 9 Aug 2026 - the resolution threshold is already exceeded by ~$165M (11%)

Third-biggest second weekend ever ($145M domestic, -59%, Variety 9 Aug) and $381M global sophomore frame (TheWrap 9 Aug) - crossing is corroborated by multiple independent trade outlets, not a single source
Cumulative gross is monotonically non-decreasing; 143 days remain to 31 Dec 2026 and the film is still the global No. 1

factors_down.factor: Theoretical resolution-source anomaly: both Box Office Mojo and The Numbers would have to restate the worldwide cume downward by more than $165M - no precedent among $1B+ releases
Residual ambiguity if a resolver were to insist on a specific single-source snapshot with materially different international accounting - implausible given the size of the cushion

key_uncertainties: None material to resolution: the only live uncertainty is whether the tracker's resolver formally marks the question YES now or waits for the 31 December endpoint
Small tracker-to-tracker variance in reported international gross (typically low single-digit percent), which is far smaller than the ~$165M margin above the threshold
update_triggers: No further upward revision is possible - the forecast is at 100 and the underlying event is observed
Revise DOWN only if Box Office Mojo AND The Numbers both restate the worldwide cume below $1.5B (unprecedented; would require a downward correction of more than $165M)
Revise DOWN if the tracker's resolution criteria are reinterpreted in a way that excludes the currently reported worldwide figure
Otherwise: cease active re-forecasting and mark this question resolved YES as of 9 August 2026

forecasts.question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 99, CI [98,99], unchanged from 6 August. The 6-10 August window produced no revenue-negative news and one materially positive datapoint that had not been fully priced in the prior forecast. TickerTrends' tracking note (blog.tickertrends.io, 'Anthropic Is Tracking Above OpenAI in ARR, but Its Growth Is Beginning to Decelerate', and its companion 'OpenAI ARR Growth Accelerated Into July') now puts OpenAI at $41.3-42.6B ARR as of 29 July, up from $37.3B on 25 June and $33.0B on 30 May, driven by GPT-5.6, ChatGPT Work and Codex; Sarah Friar's 29 July all-hands remark (CNBC) that July ARR topped all of Q2 and that OpenAI logged its first $1B revenue month is consistent. The prior forecast had modelled OpenAI at only ~$25B, so the conservative arm of the arithmetic strengthens: even Anthropic's official $47B (28 May Series H disclosure, $965B valuation) plus OpenAI's self-confirmed ~$2B/month (~$24B) already sums to ~$71B, and the tracked pairing ($74.1B + $42.6B) reaches ~$117B. None of the standing DOWN triggers fired. No public S-1 appeared on EDGAR for either company (Anthropic filed confidentially 1 June, OpenAI 8 June; both remain under SEC review as of 9 August). No tracker retraction or restatement occurred. No month-over-month ARR decline was reported at either firm. No product suspension. Substantive 6-10 August news was operational rather than financial: Anthropic's in-house chip design team and Norway project (7 Aug), its disclosure that three Claude models touched real organisations' systems during a mis-configured cybersecurity evaluation (7 Aug), and the White House briefing labs on the finalised voluntary cyber-risk review framework (Tuesday 4 Aug). Two mild negatives noted and priced: Anthropic's month-over-month growth decelerating from ~55% in spring to mid-single digits by July, and continued commentary on its gross-basis revenue recognition. Already at the calibration cap; hold.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: probability that two companies whose combined ARR already exceeds the threshold on a conservative official-disclosure-only basis fail to be reported above it five months later. On official figures alone the sum is ~$71-72B today (Anthropic $47B run-rate, Series H disclosure 28 May 2026; OpenAI ~$2B/month self-confirmed, ~$24B annualised); on third-party tracking it is ~$117B (TickerTrends, late July 2026: Anthropic $74.1B, OpenAI $42.6B). Companies on this trajectory (Anthropic ~$9B end-2025 to $47B official May 2026; OpenAI $33.0B May to $42.6B July tracked) essentially never retrench 40%+ over two quarters absent bankruptcy-level events; historical base rate of YES for this class is >98%. Limitation: the class is thin (no prior firms have scaled this fast from this base), and both companies' headline ARR figures depend on non-standardised, self-reported or modelled methodologies rather than audited statements. Sources: Anthropic Series H disclosure 28 May 2026 (CNBC, Axios, TechCrunch); CNBC 29 July 2026 (Friar); TickerTrends ARR tracking July-August 2026; Epoch AI revenue tracker; The Information, 'OpenAI Tops $25 Billion in Annualized Revenue as Anthropic Narrows Gap'.

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 34% (CI unchanged [21,48]). The 6-10 August window produced the first genuinely on-topic evidence in weeks, but it cuts both ways and nets to roughly zero. On 6 August Bank Underground published two Bank of England staff posts. Sandra Batten's 'Is artificial intelligence making us more productive? What the UK industry data show' finds that 'Computer programming, consultancy and related activities' (SIC 62) raised its contribution to annual UK productivity growth tenfold, from 0.01pp (2010-19) to 0.10pp (2023-25), while 'Information services' (SIC 63) flipped from a drag to +0.06pp, and reports a positive but weak cross-industry association between AI adoption and improved productivity contribution (slope 0.105, p=0.065, R-squared 0.10). This is the ICT-revolution pattern starting to appear - but Batten stresses the gains sit almost entirely in the AI-producing sector, financial services still contributes negatively, and adopter-side gains historically arrive only after widespread adoption and firm reorganisation. Magnitudes (0.1pp) are an order below what is needed to lift the decade mean above 1.5%. The companion post, 'Canaries in the column?', found vacancies in the most AI-exposed occupations down 15% over three years versus 6% for least-exposed, with customer-service and admin roles down over 20% - the labour-supply offset. Actively seeking disconfirming evidence: on 7 August it emerged Demis Hassabis is stepping back as head of Google DeepMind with Alphabet consolidating AI development in California, weakening London's position; EY's August Outlook has business investment falling 0.7% in 2026 with 2027-28 investment growth revised down to 1.8% and 2.6%; Calastone reported GBP 1.6bn of July equity-fund outflows (GBP 13.9bn over 12 months) on tax uncertainty; Lloyds put July house-price growth at 0.1%, weakest since November 2023; and public debt is near GBP 3trn (~95% of GDP). Gilts drifted to ~5.07% on 10-year as Brent held above USD 83 with Hormuz talks stalled - neither the UP trigger (below 4%) nor the DOWN trigger (above 5.5%) fired. No OBR, IMF or OECD long-run revision landed. No trigger fired; hold.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class: UK decade-average annual real GDP growth - 2.9% (1980s), 2.1% (1990s), 1.8% (2000s including the GFC), 2.0% (2010s), and roughly 1.3-1.5% for the 2020s to date; only 2 of the last 4 completed decades cleanly exceeded 1.5%, and post-2008 trend growth has sat near 1-1.5% for over 15 years (ONS ABMI series; House of Commons Library CBP-9040). Institutional projections cluster at or below the bar: OBR expects average growth of about 1.5% per year from 2027 onwards after the productivity downgrade (OBR EFO, with a further downgrade in March 2026), IMF 2026 Article IV puts UK potential at about 1.4%, OECD's July 2026 UK survey urges stronger productivity growth and forecasts 0.9% (2026) and 1.1% (2027), and EY's August 2026 Outlook has 0.9% (2026) and 1.2% (2027). Exceeding a 1.5% mean for a full decade therefore requires a genuine productivity regime change (AI diffusion) or sustained catch-up. Limitations: decade means are a small sample (n=5 modern decades), definitions and ONS revisions shift the measured mean by a few tenths, and none of these institutional forecasts extends to 2039, so the 2030s view is an extrapolation of trend plus a technology-shock term.

factors_up.factor: BoE staff evidence (Bank Underground, 6 Aug 2026) that AI-producing sectors are already lifting UK productivity contributions (SIC 62 from 0.01pp to 0.10pp; SIC 63 from negative to +0.06pp), consistent with the early phase of a general purpose technology cycle whose adopter-side gains would land in the 2030s
BoE scenarios converge to 1.6-1.7% annual growth by 2028-29, giving positive momentum into the decade
Large committed UK AI infrastructure capex (Microsoft, Nvidia, Nscale, BlackRock) raising the capital stock entering the 2030s, plus an active government adoption push
Alternative RTI-based productivity measures suggest a stronger underlying trend than LFS-based series imply; post-energy-shock normalisation and catch-up in the early 2030s

factors_down.factor: Official potential-growth estimates (OBR ~1.5% from 2027, IMF potential ~1.4%, OECD ~1%) all at or below the bar, and the OBR's central AI uplift is only about 0.2pp/yr; Batten's measured AI gains are 0.1pp and concentrated in AI-producing sectors, with financial services still a negative contributor

Investment channel weak: EY (Aug 2026) has business investment falling 0.7% in 2026 with 2027-28 growth revised down; 10-year gilt at ~5.07% (G7-high) with Brent above USD 83 on stalled Hormuz talks; record GBP 13.9bn 12-month equity fund outflows on tax uncertainty; debt near GBP 3trn (~95% of GDP)
Demographics: shrinking workforce growth, lower net migration assumptions, and rising old-age dependency through the 2030s; OBR has labour supply growth slowing to about 0.5%

AI's labour-market drag and possible loss of UK AI leadership: AI-exposed vacancies down 15% over three years (BoE, 6 Aug), and Alphabet consolidating DeepMind development in California (reported 7 Aug)

key_uncertainties: Whether the AI productivity gains the BoE now detects in producing sectors (0.1pp scale) broaden into AI-using sectors at multi-tenths-of-a-point scale before 2030, which is the single biggest swing factor for the decade mean
Whether the 28 October 2026 Budget under PM Burnham and Chancellor Healey retains the inherited fiscal rules, and how the accompanying OBR forecast treats trend productivity
Long-run energy costs given the Strait of Hormuz disruption and Brent above USD 83, and whether elevated gilt yields persist and suppress the capital stock entering the 2030s
Migration policy and labour-supply growth through the 2030s under a devolution-focused government
ONS measurement and revision risk (LFS versus RTI productivity divergence) around a threshold the decade mean may sit within a few tenths of
